Series::dim¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

std::int64_t Series::dim() const

What It Does¶

Returns the rank of the Series: how many coordinates are needed to address one value.

This is a purely structural question, unrelated to how many values exist or how big any one axis is. A scalar has rank 0 — no coordinates needed, there is only ever one value. A vector has rank 1. A matrix has rank 2. Every extra pair of brackets in a nested initializer, every unsqueeze, adds one more axis and therefore one more to dim().

dim() is the number every negative-axis argument elsewhere in Series normalizes against: sum(-1), cat(-1), unsqueeze(-1) all resolve -1 to dim() - 1 internally. Knowing dim() is knowing which axis “the last one” actually is for a given tensor.

The call is a plain native-integer accessor: no allocation, no data movement, and (being a scalar std::int64_t, not a Series) nothing to differentiate.

Parameters¶

None.

Returns¶

std::int64_t The number of axes in the current logical shape. Always >= 0.

Gradient¶

Not applicable — dim() returns a plain C++ integer, not a Series, so there is no sensitivity to track.

Examples¶

Example 1. Rank climbs with each level of nesting.

auto s = pluss::make_series(7.0);
auto v = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0});
auto m = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0}, {3.0, 4.0}});
auto t = m.unsqueeze(0);
std::cout << "scalar dim=" << s.dim() << "\n";
std::cout << "vector dim=" << v.dim() << "\n";
std::cout << "matrix dim=" << m.dim() << "\n";
std::cout << "3-D    dim=" << t.dim() << "\n";

Output¶

scalar dim=0
vector dim=1
matrix dim=2
3-D    dim=3

Example 2. An axis with extent 0 still counts toward rank — dim() counts axes, not the values along them.

auto e = pluss::series::zeros({2, 0, 4});
std::cout << "shape=[2,0,4] dim=" << e.dim() << ", numel=" << e.numel() << "\n";

Output¶

shape=[2,0,4] dim=3, numel=0

Three axes, zero values — the two counts answer entirely different questions. See numel for the value-count side of this distinction.

Example 3. dim() and numel() vary independently: a “wide” rank-1 tensor can hold more values than a “deep” high-rank one.

auto wide = pluss::series::zeros({1000});
auto tiny_deep = pluss::series::zeros({1, 1, 1, 1, 1});
std::cout << "wide:      dim=" << wide.dim() << ", numel=" << wide.numel() << "\n";
std::cout << "tiny_deep: dim=" << tiny_deep.dim() << ", numel=" << tiny_deep.numel() << "\n";

Output¶

wide:      dim=1, numel=1000
tiny_deep: dim=5, numel=1

Example 4. Shape-changing views alter dim() without moving a single value.

auto m = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0}, {3.0, 4.0}});
auto flat = m.reshape({4});
auto boxed = m.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0);
std::cout << "m     dim=" << m.dim() << "\n";
std::cout << "flat  dim=" << flat.dim() << "\n";
std::cout << "boxed dim=" << boxed.dim() << "\n";

Output¶

m     dim=2
flat  dim=1
boxed dim=4

reshape collapses two axes into one; each unsqueeze inserts a new length-1 axis. All three share the same four underlying values.

Example 5. dim() is exactly what a negative axis argument resolves against, everywhere in Series.

auto t = pluss::series::zeros({2, 3, 4});
std::cout << "sum(-1) reduces axis " << (t.dim() - 1) << "\n";
auto r = t.sum(-1);
std::cout << "result sizes=[" << r.size(0) << "," << r.size(1) << "]\n";

Output¶

sum(-1) reduces axis 2
result sizes=[2,3]

-1 on a rank-3 tensor means axis 2 — one less than dim() — which is why the result drops that axis and keeps [2, 3].

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • dim() == 0 means “no axes” (a scalar), not “empty”. Test emptiness with numel == 0 instead.

  • dim() == 1 means “one axis of any extent”, not “exactly one value” — a length-1000 vector still has rank 1.

  • An axis of extent 0 still counts toward rank; see Example 2.

  • dim() reflects the current view. Reshaping, squeezing, or unsqueezing changes it immediately and without copying data.

Summary¶

dim() returns the Series’ rank — the number of axes, independent of how many values exist or how big any one axis is:

  • scalar 0, vector 1, matrix 2, and so on

  • independent of numel; a wide rank-1 tensor can outnumber a deep high-rank one

  • what every negative-axis argument elsewhere resolves against

  • no allocation, no gradient — a plain integer accessor

See Also¶

  • Series::numel: the value count — the complementary structural question to rank.

  • Series::size / Series::sizes: the extent of one axis, or all of them.

  • Series::stride: how coordinates on each axis map to storage.
